title: What is the difference between role-based and policy-based authorization?
description: When roles are enough, when you need policies, and how to write a custom authorization handler.

data.text: **Question:** What is the difference between role-based and policy-based authorization?

Role-based authorization checks a single claim value: *is the user in role X?* Policy-based authorization evaluates a **named set of requirements** through pluggable handlers — a policy can combine roles, claims, and custom business rules (tenure, MFA, resource ownership). Roles are a special case of policies; anything a role check can do, a policy can do, plus everything roles cannot express.

**Role-based:**
- `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin,Manager")]` — string comparison against role claims
- Simple, readable, fine for coarse groups (Admin, User, Moderator)
- Degrades badly as rules grow: role explosion ("Admin-US-Readonly"), business rules that are not roles, and role strings scattered through the codebase

**Policy-based:**
- A policy is a named collection of **requirements**; each requirement has one or more **handlers** that call `context.Succeed(...)`
- Built-in requirements: role, claim (with value matchers), authentication scheme
- Custom requirements carry any rule you model — years of tenure, verified email, region
- Handlers are registered in DI, are unit-testable in isolation, and keep rules out of controllers
- `[Authorize(Policy = "CanEditDocument")]` reads as intent, not mechanism

**Choosing between them:**
- Coarse, stable groups → roles (or a simple built-in policy wrapping a role)
- Combinations, conditionals, or data-dependent rules → custom policies
- Per-record decisions ("may this user edit THIS document") → resource-based authorization: pass the resource to `[Authorize(Policy, Resource = doc)]` or call `IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync` — do not mint a policy per record

data.title: Custom requirement and handler

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Knowing roles are just claims, and policies generalize them
- Practical experience: when a simple role check stopped being enough
- Understanding of requirements/handlers and where they live (DI, not controllers)
- Awareness of resource-based authorization for ownership checks

items: Scattering `if (user.IsInRole("Admin"))` through controllers instead of declaring intent once
Creating one policy per user or per record — policies are named application rules, not queries
Forgetting to register the handler: the policy compiles but authorization throws or always denies
Failing the whole policy from one handler instead of letting each requirement succeed independently
Trusting role claims that originated from the client without validating them at authentication time
How does resource-based authorization differ from a global policy?
What is a fallback policy and when would you set one?
How would you unit test an authorization handler?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Roles check one claim; policies evaluate named, composable requirements
Custom requirements + handlers keep rules out of controllers and are testable
Use resource-based authorization for per-record ownership checks
Register handlers in DI and consider a fallback policy for unauthenticated requests
data.takeaway: Model authorization as named policies with requirements and handlers — roles stay as one requirement among many instead of the whole system.
